passage.title: Screens, Sleep and Study
paragraphs: Most university students carry a small computer in their pocket every day. They use their phones to send messages, to listen to music, and to look for information for their classes. Technology helps them, but it also creates new problems.

Doctors say that many students sleep badly because they check their phones in bed. The light from the screen tells the brain that it is still daytime, so the student is not sleeping when the body needs to rest. In the morning, that student always feels tired, and he or she often forgets what the teacher explained the day before.

Some universities are trying a simple solution. Students leave their phones in a box at the door of the classroom, and they only use them during the break. The teachers say the classroom is quieter now and the students are participating more.

Of course, nobody is going to stop using technology, and nobody should. Phones are not the enemy. The important question is not "How much technology do you use?" The important question is "When do you use it?" Experts believe that small changes will make a big difference: no screens thirty minutes before bed, and no phones during class. Are you going to try it?

passage.title: The Bicycle That Changed a City
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, the streets of Bogotá, Colombia, were full of cars. Every morning, thousands of people spent two hours in traffic to arrive at work. The air was dirty and the drivers were angry.

Then the city built something simple: a network of bicycle paths. Today those paths are more than five hundred kilometers long, and every Sunday the city closes its main avenues to cars. Families walk, run and ride their bicycles in the middle of the street.

The idea was not expensive, but it changed the way people move. Many workers now arrive at the office in thirty minutes instead of two hours. Other cities in Latin America are copying the plan, and experts believe more capitals will close their streets to cars on Sundays in the next few years.
